title: From Rented Cows to ₹2.4 Crore: Jaipur Couple's Gir Dairy Dream
excerpt: Vibhor and Ishita Jain started Kinaya Organic Farms in 2018 with no farming experience. Today it runs 100 Gir cows and sells A2 milk and bilona ghee.
body:
• Vibhor and Ishita Jain left corporate careers to start Kinaya Organic Farms in 2018 on leased land near Jaipur, beginning with 20 rented Gir cows and no farming experience.
  • The farm now houses 100 Gir cows and produces 250–300 litres of A2 milk and 9 litres of hand-churned bilona ghee every day.
  • Annual turnover is around ₹2.4 crore, built on a direct-to-consumer model that sells indigenous-cattle dairy — milk, bilona ghee, and cultured products — at premium prices.
  • The couple's mission doubles as conservation: the number of 100% pure Gir cows in India is critically low, estimated at only around 3,000 animals.

No land, no experience, twenty cows

In 2018, Vibhor Jain did what most parents in Jaipur would call unthinkable. The computer science graduate walked away from the prospect of a corporate career, leased a patch of land about 35 kilometres from the city, and started a dairy farm with 20 rented Gir cows. No one in his family had ever farmed. His wife Ishita, an engineer with an MBA, joined him in the venture. Eight years later, Kinaya Organic Farms houses 100 Gir cows and turns over roughly ₹2.4 crore a year.

The farm's daily output tells the story of scale: 250 to 300 litres of A2 milk and 9 litres of pure bilona ghee every single day. It is a long way from the couple's first season, when Vibhor was still learning how to keep cattle alive.

Why Gir, and why it matters

The breed choice was deliberate. Vibhor became convinced that indigenous cattle — desi cows — were both a better business and a better product. Gir cows, the hardy breed from Gujarat's Kathiawad region, produce milk rich in the A2 beta-casein protein variant. Indigenous-cattle advocates argue that A2 milk is easier to digest than the A1 milk from hybrid and Jersey cows; Ishita has said that customers who considered themselves lactose-intolerant found the farm's A2 milk easier on their stomachs.

There is also a conservation argument. The number of 100% pure Gir cows in India is estimated at only around 3,000 animals, and Vibhor watched the count of genuine purebreds declining. In 2017, before starting the farm, he travelled to Kathiawar in Gujarat to learn livestock-rearing practices from families who had raised indigenous cattle for generations — and noticed that those farmers, despite owning excellent cattle, were forced to sell milk and ghee at very low prices because they lacked access to urban markets. That gap became his business plan.

Building trust, litre by litre

The couple's early moves were pragmatic. They rented before they bought, learned before they scaled, and after three years of operations purchased their own land, moving the farm to a 12-acre property. Marketing, though, is where the engineers' instincts showed. Vibhor used Facebook and YouTube to document the farm's daily routine — the milking, the feeding, the ghee-making — building a direct relationship with customers who could watch exactly where their milk came from. Gir cow milk sells at around ₹125 per litre, a premium that only works when buyers trust the source.

The product strategy leaned into value addition rather than volume. Instead of selling liquid milk wholesale, the Jains focused on higher-margin products: bilona ghee, made by hand-churning cultured curd the traditional way, along with other cultured dairy products. They have since invested around ₹30 lakh in freeze-drying equipment to make shelf-stable formats that travel without cold-chain logistics — technology applied to a very old craft.

The bigger picture for Indian dairy

Kinaya sits inside a larger shift. India's dairy giants have long run on high-volume, low-margin milk, but a growing urban middle class is willing to pay for provenance: A2 milk, bilona ghee, desi-breed sourcing. First-generation agripreneurs like the Jains — young, educated, tech-comfortable — are professionalising the farm-to-doorstep model that earlier generations ran informally. Their ₹2.4-crore turnover, on 100 cows, is a working answer to the question of whether small, sustainable, indigenous-cattle dairy can be a serious business rather than a lifestyle project.

What's next

With the freeze-dried line expanding their reach beyond Jaipur's delivery radius, the couple's next chapter is distribution: taking indigenous-cattle dairy to customers who will never visit the farm but will pay for what it stands for. If they succeed, the blueprint travels — rented cows, leased land, and a camera phone may be all the next agripreneur needs.
